summary.text: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the historical northern borders of Chinese states as protection against nomadic groups from the Eurasian Steppe.
The first walls date to the 7th century BC and were joined together in the Qin dynasty, and successive dynasties expanded the system.
The best-known sections were built by the Ming dynasty, and the whole system spans 21,196.18 km (13,170.70 mi) in total.

facts.label: Earliest walls
facts.value: 7th century BC, joined together under the Qin

facts.label: Best-known sections
facts.value: Built by the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644)

facts.label: Watchtowers
facts.value: Up to 25,000 estimated on the wall

facts.label: Recognition
facts.value: UNESCO World Heritage Site; New 7 Wonders vote in 2007

items.prompt: After unification, Qin's ruler tore down the walls that divided the former states. Why did he still order new wall-building in the north?

options.label: To mark a permanent border that would never move
To connect the remaining northern fortifications against the Xiongnu
To keep former feudal lords apart from each other
To collect duties on goods moving along the Silk Road

items.explain: To position the empire against the Xiongnu, he ordered new walls connecting the remaining fortifications along the northern frontier, and it was not meant as a permanently fixed border.

items.prompt: A work crew must build a wall segment across a flat plain far from any stone. Following the builders' approach, which material fits?

options.label: Hauled-in stone
Fired brick
Imported timber
Rammed earth

items.explain: Builders used local resources: stone in montane areas and rammed earth in the plains.

items.prompt: After a defeat by the Oirats at the Battle of Tumu, amid long conflict with Mongol tribes, how did the Ming change their defense?

options.label: They built walls along the northern border
They abandoned the north and moved the capital
They tore down older walls to trade freely
They relied on watchtowers in the south alone

items.explain: A new strategy for defense was realized by constructing walls along the northern border of China.

items.prompt: Why was Ming construction stronger and more elaborate than earlier fortifications?

options.label: Builders packed earth and gravel between board frames
Builders used timber for the whole structure
Builders used bricks and stone instead of rammed earth
Builders relied on local mud alone

items.explain: Earlier walls were mostly stone or stamped earth and gravel between board frames, whereas the Ming used bricks and stone instead of rammed earth.

items.prompt: Why did dynasties after Qin usually avoid calling their own additions the 'Long Wall'?

options.label: The name was tied to the First Emperor's supposed tyranny
The name was reserved for walls made of stone
European travelers had already named it differently
The name meant a city rampart, not a border

items.explain: Because of the wall's association with the First Emperor's supposed tyranny, later dynasties usually avoided the name Long Wall for their own additions.

items.prompt: A guard post on the wall stops a caravan and charges a fee on its goods. Which purpose of the wall is this?

options.label: Signaling by smoke or fire
Border control, including duties on goods
Housing troops in barracks
Serving as a transportation corridor

items.explain: Beyond defense, the wall served for border controls, including the imposition of duties on goods transported along the Silk Road.
